turns.q: whats the limit of (x^2-1)/(x-1) as x->1
turns.ans: The limit is 2. Direct substitution gives 0/0, so factor and simplify first. 1) Factor the numerator: x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1). 2) Cancel the common factor (x - 1), which is allowed because x approaches 1 but never equals 1, so (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) equals x + 1 for every x near 1. 3) Substitute x = 1 into x + 1: 2.

turns.expect: Factor to (x-1)(x+1)/(x-1) = x+1 for x != 1, then plug in x = 1 to get 2.
turns.ans: We got it by simplifying the fraction first, because putting x = 1 straight in gives 0/0, which doesn't tell us the limit. 1) Factor the top using difference of squares: x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1). 2) Cancel the common factor (x - 1). This is allowed because x gets close to 1 but never equals 1, so (x^2 - 1)/(x - 1) equals x + 1 for every x near 1. 3) Now substitute x = 1 into the simpler expression: 1 + 1 = 2. As a check, try x = 1.01: (1.01^2 - 1)/(1.01 - 1) = 2.01, which is very close to 2.

turns.ans:
Mitosis and meiosis are both ways cells divide, but they do different jobs.

Mitosis makes two genetically identical daughter cells with the same number of chromosomes as the parent. It's used for growth, repair and replacing worn-out cells.
Meiosis makes four genetically varied daughter cells, each with half the chromosome number. It's used to make sex cells (sperm and eggs), and the shuffling of genes between parents makes each offspring unique.

A quick way to remember it: mitosis keeps things the same, meiosis mixes things up and halves them. Your planner doesn't have any course notes on this topic, so this is from general biology knowledge.

turns.expect: A red blood cell placed in salty (hypertonic) water shrinks as water leaves it.
turns.ans:
Sure! Here's a simple everyday-style example of osmosis:

Picture a red blood cell placed in pure water. The water outside is more dilute than the inside of the cell, so water moves across the cell membrane into the cell.
The cell swells as more water flows in, and it can eventually burst (lyse) if too much water enters.
Now put the same cell in a very salty solution. The outside is more concentrated, so water moves out of the cell, and the cell shrinks and becomes wrinkled (crenated).

In both cases, only water moves. The salt and other solutes stay on their own sides of the membrane.

turns.expect: Price is set where the quantity suppliers offer equals the quantity buyers want; higher prices raise supply and lower demand.
turns.ans:
Supply and demand is the core idea behind how prices get set in a market.

Demand is how much of a good people want to buy. Usually, the higher the price, the less people buy, so demand slopes downward.
Supply is how much sellers are willing to offer. Usually, the higher the price, the more sellers produce, so supply slopes upward.
Equilibrium is the point where the two curves cross. At that price, the amount buyers want matches the amount sellers offer.
Shifts happen when something other than price changes. For example, higher incomes can raise demand, and higher production costs can reduce supply.

If demand rises while supply stays the same, the price tends to go up. If supply rises while demand stays the same, the price tends to fall.

Sellers respond by raising the price, and the market settles at a new equilibrium with a higher price and a higher quantity.

Effects: savings lose purchasing power, fixed incomes stretch less far, and borrowers with fixed-rate debt can benefit.
Control: central banks often raise interest rates to slow it down.

turns.expect: Classical (Pavlov) pairs a neutral stimulus with a reflex-triggering one; operant (Skinner) changes behavior through rewards and punishments.
turns.ans: Classical conditioning learns an association between two stimuli, while operant conditioning learns an association between a behavior and its consequences. I checked your notes, files and marked work and found nothing on this topic, so here is the general explanation. Classical conditioning comes from Pavlov. A neutral stimulus, like a bell, is repeatedly paired with a stimulus that naturally triggers a response, like food causing salivation. Eventually the bell alone triggers salivation. The response is involuntary and reflexive. Operant conditioning comes from B.F. Skinner. A behavior becomes more or less likely depending on what follows it. Reinforcement (positive or negative) increases a behavior, and punishment decreases it. The learner actively does something to get a result. Quick way to remember it: classical is about what comes before a response (stimulus pairing), and operant is about what comes after a behavior (consequences). turns.expect: Sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational.
turns.ans:
Piaget's theory describes four stages of cognitive development that children move through in order:

Sensorimotor (birth to about 2): Babies learn by using their senses and movements. They develop object permanence, the understanding that things still exist when out of sight.
Preoperational (about 2 to 7): Children begin using symbols, words, and pretend play, but their thinking is still egocentric and they struggle with conservation (seeing that a quantity stays the same when its shape changes).
Concrete operational (about 7 to 11): Children think logically about concrete objects and events, and they understand conservation and reversibility.
Formal operational (about 11 and up): Teens and adults can reason abstractly, test hypotheses, and think about ideas that aren't tied to real objects.

turns.expect: English physicist/mathematician who formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation (Principia, 1687) and co-invented calculus.

Isaac Newton (1643 to 1727) was an English mathematician, physicist, astronomer and alchemist, and one of the most influential scientists who ever lived. He is best known for three things:

Laws of motion: he described how forces change the movement of objects, the basis of classical mechanics.
Universal gravitation: he showed the same force pulls an apple to the ground and keeps the Moon orbiting the Earth.
Calculus: he developed it independently of Leibniz, and used it to explain planetary motion.

His main work, the *Principia Mathematica* (1687), shaped physics for centuries. He also built one of the first practical reflecting telescopes and served as Master of the Royal Mint later in life.

turns.expect: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, independently.

Newton worked out his ideas earlier, in the 1660s, but published later, which led to a long priority dispute between the two. Today both are credited, and Leibniz's notation (like the integral sign and dy/dx) is the one most used now.

turns.expect: SA node to AV node to bundle of His to Purkinje fibers.
turns.ans:
The cardiac conduction pathway is the route an electrical impulse takes through your heart, and it's what makes the chambers contract in a coordinated order.

Here's the path, in order:

SA node (sinoatrial node): the heart's natural pacemaker, in the right atrium. It fires the impulse, usually 60 to 100 times a minute at rest.
Atria contract: the impulse spreads across both atria, pushing blood into the ventricles.
AV node (atrioventricular node): in the floor of the right atrium. It briefly delays the signal so the ventricles have time to fill.
Bundle of His: the only electrical link between atria and ventricles, running down the septum.
Left and right bundle branches: split the signal down each side of the septum.
Purkinje fibers: spread the impulse through the ventricular walls, so the ventricles contract from the apex upward and push blood out.

A quick memory trick: SA, AV, Bundle, Branches, Purkinje. I don't have your lecture notes for Quiz 4 in your planner, so I've given the standard version. If you share the slides or chapter, I can check it against your course material and make flashcards for each step.

turns.q: what's the difference between systole and diastole
turns.expect: Systole: ventricles contract and eject blood; diastole: ventricles relax and fill.
turns.ans:
Systole is the phase when the ventricles contract and push blood out, and diastole is the phase when they relax and fill with blood again.

turns.expect: Albert Ellis's rational-emotive behavior therapy: dispute irrational beliefs (musts, shoulds) using the ABC model.
turns.ans:
REBT stands for Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy, a form of cognitive behavioral therapy developed by psychologist Albert Ellis in the 1950s. Its core idea is the ABC model: an Activating event happens, we form Beliefs about it, and those beliefs lead to Consequences like emotions and behaviors. REBT holds that it is often our irrational beliefs, such as demands that things must go perfectly, rather than the events themselves, that cause distress. Therapists help people notice these beliefs, challenge them with evidence and logic, and replace them with more flexible, rational ones.

If you're studying it for a course, I can help you make flashcards or a short summary once you share the relevant notes or file.

turns.expect: Activating event, Belief, Consequence.
turns.ans:
The ABC model is the core of REBT: A is the Activating event, B is the Belief you form about it, and C is the Consequence, meaning the emotions and behaviors that follow.

A (Activating event): something that happens, like a missed deadline or a critical comment.
B (Belief): how you interpret that event. REBT focuses on irrational beliefs, often shown as musts and shoulds, such as "I must never fail."
C (Consequence): the feelings and actions that result, such as anxiety or avoiding work.

In REBT, the belief (B) is what drives the consequence (C), not the event (A) alone. Therapy then disputes the irrational B and replaces it with a more rational one.

This is from your sticky note on Rational-emotive behavior therapy (Albert Ellis).

turns.expect: Summarises Freud's id/ego/superego, defense mechanisms, the therapeutic relationship and REBT.
turns.ans:
Here's a summary of your psych notes, pulled from your sticky notes and the Psych Nursing Terms deck.

Freud's structure of personality: The id is the unconscious, primitive part that seeks immediate gratification (the pleasure principle) and is present from birth. The ego is the rational part that mediates between the id and reality (the reality principle) and uses defense mechanisms. The superego is the moral conscience, built from rules learned from parents and society, and it causes guilt.
Defense mechanisms: Repression pushes painful thoughts out of awareness. Projection attributes your own unacceptable feelings to someone else. Displacement redirects emotion to a safer target. Rationalization makes excuses that sound logical. Sublimation channels urges into acceptable activities.
Therapeutic relationship: Transference is when the patient unconsciously redirects feelings about someone from their past onto the nurse. Countertransference is the nurse's own emotional reaction, based on their past relationships. Nurses must recognize it and seek supervision. Peplau's phases are orientation, working, and termination.
Rational-emotive behavior therapy (Albert Ellis): The goal is to identify and dispute irrational beliefs (musts and shoulds) and replace them with rational ones, using the ABC model: Activating event, Belief, Consequence.

turns.q: teach me the cardiac cycle like i'm 5
turns.expect: Gives a simple explanation of the heart squeezing (systole) and relaxing to fill (diastole) with the SA node as the pacemaker.
turns.ans:
Sure! Imagine your heart is a little pump with four rooms. The top two rooms are called atria, and the bottom two are called ventricles.

Each heartbeat happens in two main steps:

Filling (relaxing): The heart rests and blood flows in from the body and lungs, filling the rooms like a bucket filling with water.
Squeezing (pumping): First the top rooms squeeze and push blood down into the bottom rooms. Then the bottom rooms squeeze hard and push blood out to the whole body and to the lungs.

Then the heart rests again, and the cycle starts over. It keeps doing this about 60 to 100 times every minute when you're resting!

turns.q: explain displacement with a nursing example
turns.expect: Gives a clinical example of a patient redirecting anger to a safer target.
turns.ans:
Displacement is when someone redirects a strong emotion onto a safer target than the one that actually caused it.

From your sticky note on defense mechanisms: "Displacement: redirecting emotion to a safer target (angry at boss, yells at dog)."

Nursing example:

A patient is furious about a long wait for discharge paperwork, but they feel unsafe confronting the physician, so they snap at the nurse over a small thing like the room temperature.
The anger is really aimed at the physician or the situation. The nurse becomes the safer target.

What to do: stay calm, acknowledge the feeling ("It sounds like you're really frustrated about waiting"), and help the patient name the real source of the anger. Note the pattern in the chart if it keeps happening.

Displacement is easy to mix up with transference, so keep it distinct: displacement is about a current emotion moved to a safer target, while transference is about feelings from a past relationship.

turns.q: go through transference and the id with me
turns.expect: Studies those two Psych Nursing Terms cards with the student.
turns.ans:
Sure, let's go through both. The id is one of Freud's three parts of personality, and transference is a psychodynamic idea about feelings moving from one person onto another.

The id: It's the most primitive part of the mind and is mostly unconscious. It holds basic drives like hunger, sexual desire, and aggression, and it works on the pleasure principle, which means it wants immediate gratification. It's present from birth. The ego (reality principle) and superego (internalized morals) develop to balance it.
Transference: This is when a person unconsciously redirects feelings, like love, anger, or dependence, from an important figure in their past, often a parent, onto someone else in the present. In therapy or nursing, a client may react to the nurse as if they were a parent or another significant person.
Countertransference: This is the helper's own emotional reaction to the client. Nurses should notice it, reflect on it, and keep professional boundaries.

turns.expect: Creates a map with id, ego and superego and how they relate.
turns.ans:
Freud's personality structure has three parts that work together, and your sticky note breaks them down like this:

Id: The unconscious, primitive part that seeks immediate gratification of instinctual drives (the pleasure principle). It is present from birth.
Ego: The rational part that mediates between the id and reality (the reality principle). It uses defense mechanisms to keep things balanced.
Superego: The moral conscience, made up of internalized rules from parents and society. It is what causes guilt.

A simple way to map it: the id wants, the superego judges, and the ego finds a realistic middle path between them.

You can connect this to your Defense mechanisms note, since those are the tools the ego uses.

turns.expect: Expands only the ego branch with reality principle and defense mechanisms.

The ego is the rational part of Freud's personality that mediates between the id's urges and the demands of reality.

From your sticky note on Freud's structure of personality:

Reality principle: The ego works by the reality principle, meaning it weighs what is actually possible and safe instead of chasing immediate pleasure the way the id does.
Mediator: It sits between the id (what I want now) and the superego (what I should do), looking for a workable middle path.
Defense mechanisms: When the id's drives and the superego's guilt clash, the ego uses defense mechanisms to manage the anxiety. These are unconscious strategies that protect the mind from distress.

A simple way to remember it: the id says "I want it," the superego says "You shouldn't," and the ego says "Let's find a way that works."

turns.expect: Creates a REBT concept map with Ellis, irrational beliefs, and the ABC model.

It holds that how we feel and act depends largely on the beliefs we hold about events, and that rigid, unhelpful beliefs can be questioned and replaced with more flexible ones. I checked your notes, files and open tasks and didn't find anything on REBT there, so this is my general explanation. The cardiac conduction pathway is the route an electrical impulse takes through the heart: sinoatrial (SA) node, then atrioventricular (AV) node, then the bundle of His, then the left and right bundle branches, and finally the Purkinje fibers, which spread the signal so the ventricles contract. turns.ans: Yes, I left out a few steps. The full pathway starts with the SA node, which sends the impulse across the atria through internodal pathways, so the atria contract first. Next it reaches the AV node, where the signal pauses briefly so the atria can empty into the ventricles. Then it goes through the bundle of His and splits into the right bundle branch and the left bundle branch, which divides into anterior and posterior fascicles. Finally the Purkinje fibers spread the signal through the ventricular muscle. turns.ans:
The ABC model is the core framework of Albert Ellis's rational-emotive behavior therapy (REBT), and it's in your sticky note on Rational-emotive behavior therapy (Albert Ellis).

A, Activating event: the situation or trigger that happens.
B, Belief: how you interpret that event, often as an irrational "must" or "should."
C, Consequence: the emotion and behavior that follow from that belief.

REBT adds a step after C: you dispute the irrational belief and replace it with a more rational one, which changes the consequence. The sticky note's goal is to identify and dispute those musts and shoulds.

turns.q: what should I do if it happens to me in clinical
turns.expect: Recognize it, reflect, and seek supervision/talk to the instructor, as their note says; maintain professional boundaries.
turns.ans:
If countertransference shows up for you during clinical, the first step is to notice it and name it to yourself, then pause and bring it to your clinical instructor or preceptor, or a supervisor, rather than acting on it.

Notice the feeling: if a patient is stirring up strong emotion (irritation, over-attachment, wanting to rescue or avoid them), treat that as information about you, not about the patient.
Keep care consistent: stick to the nursing plan and the patient's needs, and avoid making decisions while the reaction is driving you.
Step back if you need to: ask your instructor for a moment, hand off a task, or request a different assignment for that patient if it's affecting your care.
Debrief afterward: talk it through with your instructor, and write a short reflection on what triggered it, which also helps with your Reflection Journal.

turns.q: how is that different from displacement
turns.expect: Sublimation redirects the urge into a constructive, socially valued activity; displacement redirects emotion onto a safer target (yelling at the dog), not a productive outlet.
turns.ans:
Displacement and sublimation both move a feeling somewhere else, but the difference is in where it lands. Displacement redirects the emotion onto a safer target, like being angry at your boss but snapping at your dog. The new target is still a person or thing that doesn't deserve it, and the outlet isn't really productive. Sublimation redirects the urge into an acceptable, constructive activity, like turning that anger into a hard workout or writing about it.

Displacement: same feeling, safer target (boss to dog).
Sublimation: same feeling, constructive activity (anger to boxing or writing).

The displacement definition is from your sticky note on defense mechanisms. The sublimation definition in your note is short, so the workout and writing examples come from general psychology, not your notes.

The conduction system is the network of specialized heart muscle cells that generates and carries electrical impulses, making the heart beat in a coordinated way.

Sinoatrial (SA) node: the heart's natural pacemaker in the right atrium. It fires about 60 to 100 times a minute and starts each beat.
Atrial pathways and atrioventricular (AV) node: the impulse spreads across the atria, causing them to contract. The AV node briefly delays it so the atria can empty into the ventricles first.
Bundle of His and bundle branches: the impulse travels down the septum and splits into the left and right bundle branches.
Purkinje fibers: these spread the impulse through the ventricle walls, so the ventricles contract from the bottom up and push blood out.

Timing: a short pause (roughly 0.1 seconds) keeps the atrial and ventricular contractions in the right order, so the ventricles don't squeeze while the atria are still emptying.
Protection: the delay also limits how many fast impulses from the atria reach the ventricles, which helps keep the heartbeat controlled.

Sure, here's a fuller picture of why the AV node delays the impulse, building on what we just covered.

Filling the ventricles: During diastole the ventricles fill passively, but the atria give a final top-up (the "atrial kick"), adding roughly 20 to 30 percent of ventricular filling, especially when the heart is beating faster. If the ventricles contracted at the same moment, that extra volume would be lost.
Keeping the sequence right: The atria contract first, then the ventricles. The roughly 0.1 second AV delay lets the atrial contraction finish and the AV valves close before ventricular pressure rises. That prevents blood from being pushed back up into the atria.
Limiting the rate: The AV node conducts only so many impulses per second. If the atria fire very fast (as in atrial fibrillation or flutter), the AV node filters them, so the ventricles don't beat dangerously fast. This is why the AV node is called the "gatekeeper" of the ventricles.
Backup pacing: If the SA node slows or fails, the AV node and His-Purkinje system can take over as a slower backup pacemaker, typically around 40 to 60 beats a minute.

turns.expect: Albert Ellis's therapy: identify and dispute irrational beliefs (musts, shoulds) and replace with rational ones using the ABC model (Activating event, Belief, Consequence).
turns.ans:
REBT stands for Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy, developed by Albert Ellis in the 1950s. It is a form of cognitive behavioral therapy based on the idea that our emotional reactions are shaped less by events themselves and more by the beliefs we hold about those events.

The core model is the ABC framework:

A (Activating event): something that happens, like a bad grade or a critical comment.
B (Beliefs): the interpretation we attach to it, which can be rational (flexible, preference-based, like "I wish I had done better") or irrational (rigid, demanding, like "I must always succeed").
C (Consequences): the emotional and behavioral results, such as anxiety, shame, or avoidance.

REBT adds two steps: D (Disputing), where you challenge irrational beliefs by asking whether they are logical, realistic, and helpful, and E (Effective new philosophy), the more flexible belief and healthier feelings that follow.

The main irrational patterns Ellis described include demanding absolutes ("must," "should"), catastrophizing ("it would be awful"), and low frustration tolerance ("I can't stand this").

turns.expect: Example ABC: A = failing a quiz, B = 'I must never fail, I'm stupid', C = depression/avoiding studying; disputing B leads to a rational belief and healthier consequence.
turns.ans:
Here's a quick everyday example of the ABC model from REBT:

A (Activating event): You get a 57% on an A&P quiz you studied for.
B (Belief): "I must always do well, and this proves I'm bad at science."
C (Consequence): You feel ashamed and avoid opening your notes all week.

Now try D (Disputing): is "I must always do well" realistic? Probably not. A healthier belief might be: "I wanted a better mark, so I'll find what tripped me up and adjust my plan." That shift leads to E (New effect): disappointment instead of shame, and a clear next step.

turns.q: patient keeps saying 'I should be perfect, I must never make mistakes'. which therapy fits
turns.expect: REBT (Albert Ellis): identifies and disputes irrational 'musts/shoulds' and replaces them with rational beliefs.
turns.ans:
For a patient whose thinking is rigid, like "I should be perfect, I must never make mistakes," cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) fits best, especially its cognitive restructuring technique. Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT) is also a strong match, because it targets demanding "must" and "should" beliefs directly.

How it usually works:

Identify the belief and the thinking pattern behind it, such as all-or-nothing thinking or catastrophising about mistakes.
Test the belief against evidence: what happens when they make a small mistake, and how often do people actually notice?
Replace it with a more flexible belief, like "I want to do well, and mistakes are a normal part of learning."
Use behavioural experiments, such as deliberately doing a task slightly imperfectly, to show that the feared outcome doesn't occur.

If perfectionism is a major theme, CBT-E (enhanced CBT for eating disorders) and CBT for perfectionism are also worth knowing about. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) can help too, by changing the patient's relationship to the thought rather than arguing with it.

If the SA node isn't firing properly, it's the first step of the heart's conduction that's affected: the SA node is the natural pacemaker, so the electrical impulse never starts normally.

How the conduction goes when it works:

SA node (natural pacemaker) starts the impulse
AV node delays it briefly so the atria can finish contracting
Bundle of His carries it down into the ventricles
Purkinje fibers spread it through the ventricle walls so they contract

Because the SA node sets the rhythm, a failing SA node usually shows up as a slow or irregular rhythm, and the lower parts of the system may take over as a backup pacemaker at a slower rate. Both were underlying causes of WWI, but they worked differently: alliances turned a regional crisis into a continental war, while imperialism created the rivalries that made tensions build in the first place.

turns.expect: Mnemonic for SA node -> AV node -> bundle of His -> Purkinje fibers, e.g. 'Sally Always Buys Purple' (S-A-B-P), matching their note order.
turns.ans:
Here's a mnemonic for the cardiac conduction pathway:

Silly Ants Hate Lemon Rice Pudding

Each word stands for one step, in order:

Silly: SA node (sinoatrial node, the heart's natural pacemaker)
Ants: AV node (atrioventricular node, which briefly delays the signal)
Hate: Bundle of His
Lemon: Left bundle branch
Rice: Right bundle branch
Pudding: Purkinje fibers, which spread the signal through the ventricle walls

The impulse starts at the SA node, crosses the atria, pauses at the AV node, then travels down the bundle of His and both bundle branches to the Purkinje fibers. The first two words cover the SA and AV nodes together.

Here are 5 practice questions on the cardiac cycle:

What happens during atrial systole, and which valves are open at that point?
Why does ventricular systole cause the AV valves to close, and what produces the first heart sound?
During isovolumetric contraction, why does ventricular pressure rise without any change in volume?
What is the end-diastolic volume, and how does it relate to stroke volume?
During ventricular filling, what causes the ventricles to fill mostly in early diastole, and what role does atrial contraction play?

Try answering them out loud or on paper first, then I can check your answers or walk through any you find tricky.

turns.expect: Gives correct answers matching their note.
turns.ans:
Here are the answers to the 5 cardiac cycle questions. 1. Atrial systole: the atria contract and push the last of the blood into the ventricles. The AV valves (tricuspid and mitral) are open, and the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary) are closed. 2. Ventricular systole raises ventricular pressure above atrial pressure, which closes the AV valves. Their closing produces the first heart sound (S1). 3. During isovolumetric contraction all valves are closed, so the ventricle contracts without blood moving out. Pressure rises quickly until it exceeds the aortic and pulmonary pressures, which opens the semilunar valves. 4. End-diastolic volume (EDV) is the blood in the ventricle at the end of filling, about 120 mL at rest. Stroke volume is EDV minus end-systolic volume, so a larger EDV generally means a larger stroke volume (Frank-Starling law). 5. Most ventricular filling happens in early diastole as the ventricles relax and their pressure drops below atrial pressure, so blood flows in passively. Atrial contraction in late diastole adds the remaining blood, roughly 20 to 30 percent, and matters more when the heart rate is high. How did you do? If you tell me your answers, I can check them.

turns.ans:
Sure! Here's a more detailed version of Freud's structural model. It describes three interacting parts of the mind, and most of their work happens below the level of awareness.

Id: The original, instinct-driven part. It is entirely unconscious and runs on the pleasure principle, seeking immediate gratification of needs like hunger, comfort and aggression. It uses primary process thinking, meaning it doesn't track logic, time or consequences. It is present from birth.
Ego: The mediator that develops out of the id in early childhood. It is partly conscious and follows the reality principle, which means it delays gratification, plans and weighs what is actually possible. It uses secondary process thinking, which is logical and organized. When the id and superego clash, the ego manages the anxiety by using defense mechanisms such as repression, denial, rationalization, displacement and sublimation (turning a drive into something socially useful, like channeling anger into sport).
Superego: The moral branch, which forms roughly between ages 3 and 6 as a child takes in the values of parents and society. It has two parts: the conscience, which produces guilt when you break a rule, and the ego ideal, which pushes you toward how you want to be. Freud linked this formation to the Oedipus complex.

How they work together: in the cookie example, the id wants the cookie now, the superego says it's not allowed before dinner, and the ego negotiates a realistic option, such as asking first

turns.q: explain the conduction system like I'm 5
turns.expect: Simple analogy like a spark starting at the SA node (the heart's drummer), passed down a relay of wires (AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibers) to make the heart squeeze.
turns.ans:
The heart's conduction system is the electrical wiring that tells your heart when to squeeze, so it beats in a steady rhythm.

Here's the simple version:

The spark starts in a small spot at the top right of the heart called the sinoatrial (SA) node. It's the heart's natural pacemaker.
The signal spreads across the upper chambers (the atria), which squeeze and push blood down into the lower chambers.
There's a short pause at the atrioventricular (AV) node, like a tiny waiting room, so the lower chambers get filled up first.
The signal zooms down the bundle of His and along the Purkinje fibers, which are like fast wires spreading through the bottom chambers (the ventricles).
The ventricles squeeze hard and push blood out to the lungs and the rest of the body.
Then it resets and the whole thing starts again, over and over, about 60 to 100 times a minute at rest.

Think of it like a line of dominoes: one tips the next, in the right order, so the heart squeezes like a pump instead of wiggling.

This is a good one for your Heart flashcard deck, which is also a nice warm-up for Lab Report: Cardiac Cycle.

turns.expect: Ellis's REBT ABC: Activating event, Belief, Consequence.
turns.ans:
The ABC model is the core tool of rational-emotive behavior therapy (REBT), the approach from Albert Ellis that your sticky note mentions. It explains how a situation leads to how you feel. - A is the Activating event, the thing that happens. - B is the Belief you hold about it, especially rigid ones like 'I must' or 'I should'. - C is the Consequence, the feeling and behavior that follows from that belief. The idea is that B causes C more than A does. Your sticky note adds the next step: dispute the irrational beliefs and replace them with more rational ones. turns.q: ok but y does B matter

Because B is the part you can actually change. A (the event) often isn't up to you, but the belief you attach to it shapes how strongly you feel and what you do next.

Two people can face the same bad quiz result. One thinks 'this is a setback, I'll review,' the other thinks 'I must never fail, I'm a failure.'
The first feels disappointed and studies more. The second feels panicked and may avoid the material.
The event is the same, but the belief leads to very different consequences (C).

That's why REBT focuses on B: changing a rigid belief can change the whole chain, even when the situation stays the same.

turns.q: why does that matter for nursing

turns.ans:
Cardiac output matters in nursing because it tells you how well blood is reaching the body's tissues, so it helps you spot problems early.

Perfusion checks: Low cardiac output can mean less oxygen and nutrients reach organs, which shows up as low blood pressure, cool or pale skin, slow capillary refill, confusion, or low urine output.
Medication and fluid decisions: Drugs like beta-blockers, diuretics, and vasopressors all change heart rate or stroke volume, so you watch how they shift cardiac output.
Early warning signs: A drop in cardiac output can signal shock, heart failure, or bleeding, and catching it fast can prevent serious harm.
Patient teaching: For heart failure patients, understanding how the heart pumps helps you explain symptoms and why daily weights and fluid limits matter.

turns.expect: Not in notes: preload = ventricular stretch/end-diastolic volume, afterload = resistance the ventricle pumps against; general A&P knowledge.
turns.ans:
Preload is how much the ventricle's walls are stretched by blood filling the heart just before it contracts, and afterload is the resistance the ventricle has to push against to eject that blood. My notes and files don't cover this, so this is from general knowledge.

Preload: the end-diastolic volume, or how full the ventricle is at the end of filling. More stretch usually means a stronger contraction (the Frank-Starling law). Low preload can come from bleeding or dehydration, and diuretics can lower it.
Afterload: the pressure the ventricle must overcome to open the aortic or pulmonary valve. For the left ventricle it's mainly systemic vascular resistance and aortic pressure. Higher afterload makes the heart work harder and can lower stroke volume. Hypertension and vasoconstriction raise it, while vasodilators like nitrates lower it.

A simple way to remember it: preload is what fills the heart, and afterload is what the heart pushes against.

turns.q: what's the refractory period in heart muscle
turns.expect: Not in notes; period after depolarization when cardiac muscle can't be re-stimulated, preventing tetany so the heart can refill; general knowledge.
turns.ans:
The refractory period in heart muscle is the short window after a cell fires when it can't be triggered again, which keeps the heart beating in an orderly rhythm. Your Cardiac cycle note doesn't mention it, so I can't pull it from your files, but here's the general idea. Cardiac muscle has a long absolute refractory period, roughly 200 to 300 ms, which lasts through most of ventricular contraction (systole). Because of this, the muscle can't be re-stimulated during a contraction and can't go into sustained tetany the way skeletal muscle can. After that comes a brief relative refractory period, when a stronger-than-normal stimulus could trigger an extra beat. Once the cell repolarizes, it's ready to fire again, and the SA node sets the pace for the next beat.

turns.q: what are the stages of grief
turns.expect: Not in their notes; Kubler-Ross: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance; notes it's general knowledge.
turns.ans:
The stages of grief are the five stages Elisabeth Kübler-Ross described in 1969: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance.

Denial: Shock or disbelief that the loss is real.
Anger: Frustration aimed at yourself, others, or the situation.
Bargaining: Wishing things had gone differently, often with "if only" thinking.
Depression: Sadness, withdrawal, and a sense of emptiness.
Acceptance: Coming to terms with the loss and learning to live with it.

People don't move through these in a neat order, and they often return to a stage more than once. These are a common framework, not a rule. If this is about someone you've lost, or something heavy you're carrying, I'm glad to talk about it, and a counselor or someone you trust can help too.

turns.q: how do defense mechanisms relate to the ego
turns.expect: Per their notes, the ego uses defense mechanisms to protect against anxiety from id/superego/reality conflicts; lists the five from their notes.
turns.ans:
The ego uses defense mechanisms to handle the tension between the id's urges and reality. From your sticky notes, the id seeks immediate gratification (the pleasure principle), the superego pushes moral rules and causes guilt, and the ego is the rational part that mediates between the id and reality (the reality principle). When the id's wants clash with what's realistic or acceptable, the ego uses defense mechanisms to cope. For example, repression pushes painful thoughts out of awareness, projection attributes your own unacceptable feelings to someone else, displacement redirects emotion to a safer target (like being angry at your boss but yelling at the dog), rationalization makes excuses that sound logical, and sublimation channels urges into acceptable activities. So the defense mechanisms are the ego's tools for keeping things balanced.

Sublimation is generally considered the most mature defense mechanism. Your sticky notes don't rank them, but in standard psychology (Freud, and later George Vaillant's hierarchy of defenses) sublimation sits at the healthy end. Repression and projection are usually ranked among the more immature ones, since they distort reality or push feelings out of awareness. Rationalization and displacement fall somewhere in the middle.

turns.q: why does the heart need a natural pacemaker
turns.expect: The SA node generates regular impulses that coordinate contraction; HR 60-100 at rest, per their note.
turns.ans:
The heart needs a natural pacemaker so it can beat on its own, in a steady, coordinated rhythm, without waiting for signals from the brain or nerves.

SA node: Your notes and flashcards name the sinoatrial (SA) node as the heart's natural pacemaker. It fires an electrical impulse about 60 to 100 times a minute at rest.
Coordinated squeeze: The impulse spreads to the AV node, then the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers. This makes the atria and then the ventricles contract in the right order, so blood is pushed efficiently: the ventricles contract in systole and relax to fill in diastole.
Why it matters: Without one steady source setting the pace, the chambers could beat out of sync, and the heart couldn't pump blood effectively to the body.

If you're writing this up for your Lab Report: Cardiac Cycle, the SA node point fits nicely in the section on how the cycle starts.

turns.q: how does it set the rate
turns.expect: Pacemaker cells spontaneously depolarize; autonomic nervous system speeds (sympathetic) or slows (parasympathetic/vagus) the rate; general knowledge.
turns.ans:
The SA node sets the rate by how quickly its cells slowly charge up to their firing point; the quicker they reach it, the faster your heart beats.

Slow build-up: Between beats, SA node cells don't rest flat. Their electrical charge drifts upward little by little (called pacemaker potential), mostly as sodium leaks in and calcium channels open.
Firing threshold: Once the charge hits a set threshold, the cell fires an impulse and resets, then the slow climb starts again. A shorter climb means more beats per minute.
Nerve input: The SA node has no fixed speed. Sympathetic nerves (adrenaline and norepinephrine) make the climb faster when you're active or stressed. The vagus nerve (acetylcholine) slows it down when you're at rest.
Your numbers: Left alone, the SA node would fire around 100 times a minute. Vagal input brings a resting heart down to roughly 60 to 100 bpm, which matches the normal range in your Cardiac cycle note (N5).

For your Lab Report, the rate point fits well right after the SA node sentence. Just make sure you describe the slow charge build-up, not only that the SA node 'sends signals'.

turns.q: explain the B in the ABC model
turns.expect: Belief: the person's interpretation of the activating event; in REBT irrational beliefs (musts, shoulds) drive the consequence.
turns.ans:
The B stands for Belief, the core of the ABC model in rational-emotive behavior therapy from Albert Ellis. It's the way you interpret the Activating event, and it's the part you can work on.

A (Activating event): something that happens, like a missed call or a bad grade.
B (Belief): what you tell yourself about that event. Ellis focused on irrational beliefs, often shaped as musts or shoulds, such as "I must do perfectly" or "They should never disappoint me."
C (Consequence): the feelings and behaviors that follow, such as anxiety, guilt, or avoiding the task.

The model's key idea is that the belief, not the event alone, drives much of the consequence. The therapy then asks you to dispute the irrational belief and replace it with a more rational one, like "I'd like to do well, but one mark doesn't define me."

This is from your sticky note on Rational-emotive behavior therapy (Albert Ellis).

turns.expect: Rigid, absolute demands (must/should), awfulizing, low frustration tolerance, global self-rating; their note mentions musts and shoulds.
turns.ans:
A belief is irrational in Ellis's view when it is rigid, absolute and demanding, usually framed as a must, should or have-to, and when it doesn't fit the facts or helps you feel worse without helping you act.

Ellis pointed to a few common signs:

Absolute demands: "I must do perfectly" or "They should never disappoint me" insist that things go a certain way.
Catastrophizing: treating a setback as the end of the world, like "If I fail this, my whole course is ruined."
Global labels: judging your whole self from one event, like "One bad mark means I'm stupid."
Low tolerance for discomfort: believing you can't stand something that is merely hard or unpleasant.

A useful test is to ask whether the belief is true, whether it helps you reach your goals, and whether it leads to a reasonable feeling. If not, you dispute it and replace it with a more flexible version, like "I'd like to do well, and if I don't, I can learn from it."

Your sticky note on Rational-emotive behavior therapy (Albert Ellis) covers the core goal of disputing these musts and shoulds.

REBT (Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy, Albert Ellis) would treat that statement as a belief to examine, not a fact to argue with head-on. Here's the usual approach:

Identify the activating event and the belief: Something like "I didn't parent well" (event) leads to "I should have been a better mom, so I'm a failure" (belief). The ABC model is A (activating event), B (belief), C (emotional and behavioural consequence, such as hopelessness or withdrawal).
Spot the musts and global labels: REBT targets demanding "should/must" thinking and global self-rating. The jump from one mistake to "I'm a failure" is the key target, because a person is not reducible to their actions.
Dispute the belief (D): The clinician asks Socratic questions: Where is the evidence that one shortcoming makes someone a failure? Is it realistic to be a perfect parent? What would I say to a friend who said this? Does this belief help me or keep me stuck?
Develop a more rational, flexible alternative (E): For example, "I wish I had handled some things differently, and I can still learn and make amends. My worth doesn't depend on being flawless."
Behavioural homework: Plan one small, concrete repair action with their child or a caring step, to test the belief against real experience.

Ego: the rational part that mediates between the id and reality (the reality principle).
Superego: the moral conscience, made of internalized rules from parents and society, which causes guilt.

Defense mechanisms

Repression: pushing painful thoughts out of awareness.
Projection: attributing your own unacceptable feelings to someone else.
Displacement: redirecting emotion to a safer target, like being angry at your boss and yelling at the dog.
Rationalization: making excuses that sound logical.
Sublimation: channeling urges into acceptable activities.

Therapeutic relationship

Transference: the patient unconsciously redirects feelings about someone from their past onto the nurse.
Countertransference: the nurse's emotional reaction to the patient, based on the nurse's own past relationships. Nurses must recognize it and seek supervision.
Peplau's phases: orientation, working, termination.

Rational-emotive behavior therapy (Albert Ellis)

Goal: identify and dispute irrational beliefs (musts and shoulds) and replace them with rational ones.
ABC model: Activating event, Belief, Consequence.

Your "Psych Nursing Terms" deck has flashcards for transference, the id, sublimation and projection if you want to test yourself on them.

turns.q: explain the musts and shoulds in REBT
turns.expect: Ellis's irrational demands about self, others and the world (e.g. 'I must succeed'), which REBT disputes; per their note.
turns.ans:
In REBT (Albert Ellis), the musts and shoulds are the rigid, absolute demands people place on themselves, others, or the world, like "I must succeed" or "they should always treat me fairly." Ellis saw these as irrational beliefs at the root of much distress, because reality rarely obeys them.

How it works:

Musts/shoulds: demands stated as fact ("I must get this right," "people should never criticize me").
Dispute them: ask whether the demand is actually true, whether it helps you, and whether it fits the evidence.
Replace them: swap the demand for a flexible preference, like "I want to get this right, and it would be hard if I didn't."

This fits the ABC model from your sticky note: the Activating event happens, your Belief (the must or should) shapes how you feel, and that gives the Consequence. Disputing the belief changes the consequence.

turns.q: give me 3 examples and the rational version
turns.expect: Three irrational musts/shoulds with rational alternatives (preferences rather than demands).
turns.ans:
Here are three common musts and shoulds, each with a more flexible, rational version you can swap in:

Must: "I must get top marks on every exam." Rational: "I want to do well on exams, and a lower score would be disappointing, but it wouldn't mean I'm incapable."
Should: "People should always be fair to me." Rational: "I'd prefer people to be fair, and when they aren't, it's frustrating, but I can still handle it."
Must: "I can't stand it if my plan falls apart." Rational: "Plans sometimes change, and that's annoying, but I can adjust and keep going."

Try this with your own belief: write the must or should, then ask if it's really true, whether it helps you, and what a flexible preference would sound like.

turns.q: i didnt get transference in class
turns.expect: Reassures them and briefly explains transference accurately from their notes (patient redirects past feelings onto the nurse).
turns.ans:
No worries, transference is a tricky one, and you can get it now.

In short, transference is when a patient unconsciously redirects feelings they had about someone from their past onto the nurse. The patient might react to you as if you were a parent, sibling or old partner, even though you're just their nurse.

Example: A patient keeps snapping at you the way they used to snap at a parent who was always critical.
Why it matters: Nurses need to notice it and not take it personally. It's also why nurses are encouraged to seek supervision.
Don't mix it up with countertransference: that's the nurse's own emotional reaction to the patient, based on the nurse's past relationships.

If it helps, try saying it back in your own words, then check it against your flashcard.

The SA node is the heart's natural pacemaker: it starts each heartbeat by firing an electrical impulse.

From your sticky note on the cardiac cycle (BIOS 230), the path goes like this:

The SA node (sinoatrial node) fires the impulse, setting the pace of your heart rate.
The impulse travels to the AV node, then the bundle of His, then the Purkinje fibers.
That pathway makes the ventricles contract, which ejects blood (systole). Then they relax and fill (diastole).

Your note also gives a normal resting heart rate of 60-100 bpm. If your lab question asks about the SA node, start with that first step of the pathway and then trace where the impulse goes next.

Its impulse triggers atrial contraction first.
The impulse then goes through the AV node, bundle of His, and Purkinje fibers to contract the ventricles.

If your lab asks why the SA node is the pacemaker, a good check is whether it fires faster than other areas of the heart, which is why it normally controls the rhythm.
